text: Someone or something venerated is treated with deep respect, often close to reverence, because of age, achievement or holiness. Napoleon's marshals were meant to be the army's most venerated figures, so the title came with honor and ceremony as well as power.

To galvanise people is to shock or excite them into action, as if giving them a jolt of electricity. Napoleon coached his marshals on how to galvanise their soldiers, meaning stir them up so they would fight harder.
To be bereft of something is to be left without it, especially something you badly need or love. At Waterloo Napoleon was bereft of the support of nearly all his marshals.
Derring-do is old-fashioned, showy bravery and daring action, the kind found in adventure stories. Caesar used his swimming across rivers to show off his derring-do to his troops.
Oppression is the cruel and unfair use of power to keep people down. The writer says to put it aside so we can look only at the management skills of conquerors.
Solidarity is standing together with others and sharing their hardships to show you are on their side. Alexander refused water before battle in solidarity with his thirsty men.
When an army wobbles, it begins to lose its nerve and may break and run, like a shaky table about to fall. Caesar rushed in front of wobbling soldiers to stop them fleeing.
Suetonius was a Roman historian who lived around the year 100 and wrote biographies of the emperors, including Julius Caesar.
Diocletian was a Roman emperor around the year 300 who split the huge empire into parts run by several rulers, while keeping the final say for himself.
A prolific writer or artist produces a great deal of work. Andrew Roberts has written many books.
The House of Lords is the upper chamber of the British Parliament, whose members are mostly appointed rather than elected. That is why the article calls the author Lord Roberts.
To proclaim something is to announce it publicly and officially. Napoleon proclaimed himself emperor in 1804, crowning himself rather than waiting to be chosen.
A marshal of the empire was the highest military rank Napoleon created. He named 18 on the day after he became emperor and 26 in all, giving them uniforms, wealth and titles.
The pinnacle is the highest point of something, like the peak of a mountain. The marshals were the pinnacle of French society, standing at the very top.
The nobility were the class of people born into titles such as duke or count. Some marshals came from this class and others from craftsmen's families, showing that talent could win a place.
To indulge someone is to give them generous treats and favors, often more than they need. Napoleon indulged his marshals with fortunes, land and marriages into his family.
Imperial means belonging to an emperor or an empire. The marshals' batons carried the gold imperial eagles, the symbol of Napoleon's empire.
A sash is a long, wide band of cloth worn over one shoulder or around the waist, often as a sign of rank or honor.
A baton is a short stick. A marshal's baton was a ceremonial symbol of his rank, a bit like a crown for a military leader.
A set-piece battle or siege is a planned, slow contest fought on fixed ground, where armies line up and a fortress is surrounded for weeks. Napoleon preferred fewer of these and more fast movement.
Manoeuvres are skilled, planned movements of troops. Napoleon's new way of war relied on agile manoeuvres rather than slow sieges.

To live off the land means to get your food and supplies from the places you travel through, instead of hauling them behind you. This let Napoleon's army move faster than armies tied to supply wagons.
To dole something out is to hand it out in portions. Napoleon doled out lavish rewards to the marshals who did well.
Lavish means extremely generous or expensive, far beyond what is needed. Napoleon's rewards were so lavish that they included princedoms and thrones.
Louis-Alexandre Berthier was Napoleon's chief of staff and first marshal, the organized mind who turned his boss's plans into detailed orders and records.
A chief of staff is the top assistant who organizes the work of a leader's team, passing along orders and information, so the leader can focus on big decisions.
Topographical means about the shape and features of land, such as hills, rivers and coastlines. A topographical engineer draws accurate maps.
Proto- means first or early. The army's detailed reports resembled spreadsheets long before computers, tables of numbers that let a leader see everything at a glance.
The Grande Armée, French for Great Army, was Napoleon's huge main fighting force, which at its peak numbered hundreds of thousands of soldiers.
A card index is a box of cards, each holding a bit of information, sorted so you can find things quickly. It was the old-fashioned version of a database.
A performance review is a formal assessment of how well someone is doing their job, used in modern companies. The writer uses the term playfully for Napoleon's public praise and blame.
Campaign bulletins were official reports Napoleon published during a military campaign, telling France what had happened and who deserved credit or blame.
Personalised means tailored to a particular person rather than the same for everyone. Napoleon gave each marshal advice that suited him.
To fanaticise someone is to fill them with fierce, burning enthusiasm for a cause. Napoleon urged his marshal to fanaticise the soldier, which meant fire up the troops to the utmost.
Autonomy is the freedom to make your own decisions without being controlled. Napoleon cramped his marshals' autonomy, which made them less effective.
To cramp something is to squeeze or restrict it. Napoleon cramped his marshals' freedom to act.
Capricious means changing suddenly and without good reason, so you cannot predict it. Napoleon's reward scheme became capricious, since praise no longer followed good work.
A scapegoat is someone unfairly blamed for the mistakes of others. Napoleon sometimes used marshals as scapegoats for his own failures.

Creative tension is healthy friction between people or ideas that pushes them to do better. In this case Napoleon's competition between marshals went too far and turned into rivalry that damaged the team.
To be at variance with someone is to disagree or be in conflict with them. Napoleon boasted that he kept his generals at variance among themselves so each would tell on the other.
Spitefulness is the wish to hurt or annoy someone out of bitterness. Even his own biographer says Napoleon had a great capacity for it.
Austerlitz, in 1805, was one of Napoleon's greatest victories, where his army beat the combined forces of Russia and Austria in what is now the Czech Republic.
Waterloo, in Belgium in 1815, was Napoleon's final defeat. The name has since come to mean any decisive, crushing failure, as in meeting your Waterloo.
To come to blows is to start fighting physically or to quarrel fiercely. The marshals, jealous of each other's glory, began to do so.
